## Pre-lab (at home, ~30 min, strongly recommended)

Play the first four modules of [Linux Survival](https://linuxsurvival.com/welcome/) — a *simulated* terminal, impossible to break. If you want a real one in your browser: [Webminal](https://www.webminal.org/).

## One idea before you type anything

The terminal works in the same loop you have already seen twice in lectures: it reads a command, carries it out, prints the result, and waits for the next one.

It does exactly what you type. It has no way of knowing what you meant. This is the same rule you met with the Turtle, and it applies to everything in this lab.

## The map — read this aloud together before typing (5 min)

Everything stored on this computer lives in **one big tree**. A **folder** (directory) is a box that can hold files and other boxes; a **file** is a page inside a box; a **path** is an address, read from the root `/` downward:

```
/                            ← the root: everything starts here
└── home
    └── student              ← the shared home
        └── csp_labs_f26
            └── w02-l01-…    ← YOUR workspace today
```

The most important fact today is that **you are always somewhere in this tree**, and every command you type acts from wherever that is. Three commands tell you where you are and move you around:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `pwd` | prints the directory you are currently in |
| `ls` | lists what is in that directory |
| `cd somewhere` | moves you into `somewhere`; `cd ..` moves you up one level |

::: {.callout-important}
**If the machine says `No such file or directory`**, it means that the name you typed does not exist in the directory you are currently in. Retyping it will not help. Instead, do these three things in order:

1. Run `pwd` to see where you are.
2. Run `ls` to see what is actually there.
3. Use `cd` to move to the right directory, then try the command again.

Most of the errors in this lab are fixed by exactly this.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Copying commands.** The command boxes on this page have a copy button at their top-right corner. The rest of the page is for reading.

Run one box at a time, and read what the machine prints before moving to the next box. Do not paste several boxes in one go.

Note that pasting into a terminal is not Ctrl+V. Use **Ctrl+Shift+V** to paste, and **Ctrl+Shift+C** to copy from the terminal.

For short commands, type them out rather than copying them. You will remember them better.
:::

## Act 0 · Install (10 min)

The lab pack is pre-placed on each machine (ask where). If it isn't — or you're at home — fetch it from the course site:

```bash
wget https://acads-iit-jammu.github.io/csp-f26-dhavala/labs/lab01.tar.gz
```

Unpack it and run the installer:

```bash
tar xzf lab01.tar.gz
cd lab01
./install.sh
```

The installer does three things. It works out which branch you are in, by reading the machine's name and today's date. It asks for your team's roll number or numbers. Then it creates your workspace at `/home/student/csp_labs_f26/w02-l01-<branch>-sd`.

If you are practising at home, that path will not exist. The installer notices this and creates the workspace in the directory you ran it from instead. Everything else behaves the same way.

These machines are shared and are cleared between sessions. Your workspace exists for today only, so you must take your work with you at the end of the lab. Act 5 explains how.

Now walk to your workspace. **Do not type any `*`** — your workspace's exact name depends on your branch, and the installer just printed it for you under **"Next steps"**. Type the `cd` line *it* printed. It will look like this (yours may say `ee`, `me` or `mt`, and can end in `-2` if another team used this machine first):

```
cd /home/student/csp_labs_f26/w02-l01-me-sd
```

Now start the session recorder. From this point on, everything you type and everything the machine prints is written to `session.txt`. You will submit that file as part of your bundle. To stop the recorder later, type `exit`.

```bash
script session.txt
```

## Act 1 · Claim the machine (10 min)

Who are you, where are you, on what? One box per question — **predict the output before each Enter**.

Who am I? (The answer is a surprise: you are *all* `student` — remember that for Act 5.)

```bash
whoami
```

Which machine is this?

```bash
hostname
```

What operating system, exactly?

```bash
uname -a
```

How much disk is free here?

```bash
df -h .
```

Now make the machine's passport — your first *redirection*: `>` sends a command's output into a file instead of the screen, and `>>` appends instead of overwriting. Writing the passport is one step (nothing appears on screen — that's the point; it went into the file):

```bash
whoami > passport.txt
hostname >> passport.txt
uname -a >> passport.txt
df -h . >> passport.txt
```

Verifying it is the next step:

```bash
cat passport.txt
```

## Act 2 · Build the home (20 min)

Four tasks. Each one states an **ENSURES** line, which tells you what must be true when you have finished. How you get there is up to you.

Before you run any `ls`, say out loud what you expect it to print, and only then press Enter.

1. **Create a `notes/` directory — your lab notebook.** Two files will live in it: `README.txt` (one line saying what lives where in this workspace) and `answers.txt`, where you'll write your answers to the **think-questions** this sheet asks along the way (they're marked ✍️). Your notebook travels home in your bundle — we read it.
   **ENSURES:** `cat notes/README.txt` prints your line. (Tools: `mkdir`, `nano`.)

2. **Build a `practice/` tree, from nothing, yourself** — you are the one creating every directory and file here. Target shape:

   ```
   practice/
   ├── a/one.txt
   ├── a/two.txt
   └── b/one.txt
   ```

   There are rules about how each file must be made, so that you use three different commands:

   - Make the two directories with `mkdir -p practice/a practice/b`.
   - Create the first file empty, using `touch`.
   - The second file must be made as a **copy** of another file, using `cp`.
   - The third file must be **moved** into place, using `mv`. So you will need to create a file somewhere else first and then move it.

   **ENSURES:** `ls -R practice` matches the diagram above exactly. Write down what you expect it to print before you run it.

3. **Now delete the `practice/` tree.** Use `rm -ri practice`. The `-i` makes it ask before each deletion; read each question before you answer it.

   `rm` does not move files to a wastebasket. There is no undo. Get into the habit of reading what it is about to delete.

   **ENSURES:** `ls` no longer shows `practice`. Keep `notes/` — that one is part of your submission.

4. **Three ways to help yourself.** Practise each one now, so that you can use it when you are stuck later.

   - Run `man ls`, find what the `-a` option does, then press `q` to quit.
   - Run `ls --help`, which prints a shorter summary.
   - Type `pass` and then press the Tab key twice. The shell completes the filename for you.

   Between them, these answer most of the questions you would otherwise have to ask.

## Act 3 · Make it speak (15 min)

Your starter files are already in the workspace (the installer put them there). Open `hello.c` and put **your name** inside the quotes (both names, for pairs):

```bash
nano hello.c
```

Compile it (silence means success — the compiler only speaks when something is wrong):

```bash
gcc hello.c -o hello
```

Run it:

```bash
./hello
```

Run it again, capturing the output into a file this time (screen stays quiet — where did it go?):

```bash
./hello > output.txt
```

Count that file's words by *piping* it through `wc`:

```bash
cat output.txt | wc -w
```

You have now compiled and run a real C program. It uses the same `printf` you saw taken apart in the Week 1 lecture. You are not expected to understand every line of it yet; you will by Week 4.

✍️ *Think-question 1, into `notes/answers.txt`:* why the `./` in `./hello`? Run `echo $PATH` and reason it out — ask us at the end if it doesn't click.

## Act 4 · Stopping a program that will not stop (10 min)

In the Week 2 lecture, the Toy Computer got stuck in a loop and the only way out was to reset it. On a real machine there are two ways to stop a running program, and you will use both here.

The starter file `loop.c` contains a program that never finishes. This is deliberate. It produces no output, so your terminal stays readable while it runs. Compile it:

```bash
gcc loop.c -o loop
```

Run it. It will not stop on its own. Press **Ctrl-C** to stop it. That is the first of the two ways:

```bash
./loop
```

Now run it again with an `&` at the end. The `&` starts the program in the background, which means the terminal gives you a prompt back straight away and **Ctrl-C** no longer reaches the program:

```bash
./loop &
```

To stop it now, you first need its process ID, which is the number the system uses to identify a running program. `pgrep loop` prints it:

```bash
pgrep loop
```

Now stop that process by number. This is the second of the two ways. Replace `12345` with the number your own `pgrep` printed:

```bash
kill 12345
```

Check that it has stopped. If `pgrep` prints nothing, there is no such process running any more:

```bash
pgrep loop
```

If you want to see what `pgrep` is doing for you, run `ps` on its own. It lists all the running processes, and you can find your `loop` among them. On a shared machine that list is long, which is why `pgrep` is useful.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Remember this for later:** `./loop &`, `pgrep`, and `kill <PID>` are **one-time** commands. They must **NOT** go into your `replay.sh` in Act 6. That PID number was true for one moment on one machine; replayed later it could kill someone else's process.
:::

Every programmer writes a program that does not stop at some point. Now you know the two ways to deal with one.

## Act 5 · Lock up and take your work (15 min)

**Why permissions exist.** Unix was written in 1969 for machines that were shared by whole teams, and it still assumes that many people use one computer. This lab is exactly that situation.

Because of this, every file records who is allowed to do what with it. There are three groups of people and three rights:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Groups** | the file's **owner** (`u`), the owner's **group** (`g`), and **others** (`o`), meaning everyone else |
| **Rights** | **r**ead, **w**rite, and e**x**ecute |

Three groups with three rights each gives the nine letters you see in `ls -l`. For example, `rwxr-xr-x` means the owner may read, write and execute the file; the group may read and execute it; and others may read and execute it.

`chmod`, short for "change mode", is the command the owner uses to change these permissions.

1. Look at a permission string: `ls -l hello`. Decode `rwxr-xr-x` on paper: three groups of three bits — `111 101 101` = octal `755`. **This week's number systems, wearing work clothes.**

2. Try `chmod 600 passport.txt`, then `ls -l passport.txt`. ✍️ *Think-question 2, into `notes/answers.txt`:* you are *all* logged in as `student` — so who exactly did you just lock out? (Honest answer: nobody in this room. `chmod` guards between *users*, and this whole room is one user. That is what permissions really are — and why real systems give each person their own account.)

3. Stop the recorder (type `exit` — you'll see "Script done"), then run the self-check:

   ```bash
   ./check.sh
   ```

   The check lists what is missing, but not how to fix it. That part is yours.

   Lines marked `bonus-open` are **not** required today. They belong to Act 6, which you do at home.

   When the required lines are green, make your bundle. If time runs out first, make the bundle anyway — an incomplete bundle is worth more than none:

   ```bash
   ./check.sh --bundle
   ```

4. The bundle is written one directory above your workspace, with a name of the form `lab01_<rolls>_<branch>_w02.tar.gz`. This file is your submitted work.

   Take it with you. Upload it to Moodle, using the link announced in the lab, and email a copy to yourself as well. Your workspace on this machine is deleted before the next lab.

## Act 6 · Bonus, at home: your history becomes a program

Do this on any machine — extract the lab pack anywhere and `./install.sh` puts a practice workspace right where you run it.

Your shell keeps a numbered history of every command you typed. That history is a record of what happened. In this exercise you turn it into a program, which is a different thing: a record says what happened once, while a program has to work every time it is run.

Start by writing the history to a file:

```bash
history > replay.sh
```

Open it and edit — rules below:

```bash
nano replay.sh
```

::: {.callout-important}
**Read these rules before you edit `replay.sh`.**

1. Every line in the file starts with a number, for example `  501  ./hello`. Those numbers are part of the history, not part of the command. If you leave them in, the shell will try to run a program called `501`. **Delete every line number.**
2. Make the very first line exactly `#!/bin/sh`. This tells the system which interpreter should run the file.
3. **Keep** only the commands that still make sense every time they are run, such as `./hello`, `cat output.txt | wc -w` and `ls -l`.
4. **Delete** `./loop &`. Running it again would start a program that never stops, with nobody watching it.
5. **Delete** the `pgrep` and `kill <PID>` lines. That process ID was correct for one moment on one machine. Run it another day and it could stop someone else's program.
6. The self-check runs your `replay.sh` and reports the result as a bonus item.
:::

Now run it — **before** doing anything else:

```bash
./replay.sh
```

You will get `Permission denied`. This is expected. A file you have just created does not have permission to be run as a program. You have to grant that permission yourself, using the `chmod` command from Act 5:

```bash
chmod +x replay.sh
```

Now it runs:

```bash
./replay.sh
```

✍️ *Bonus question for `notes/answers.txt`:* in one line, what is the difference between a history file and a program? A history records what happened once. A program has to be correct every time it runs, which is why some lines had to be deleted.
